bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v2, 20 Jul 2023; legacy file lists NeurIPS 2023, not printed in text)

question: Can ChatGPT (two Jan-2023 versions) and GPT-4 do graduate-level natural-language mathematics, and how can this be measured at fine grain?
contributions: GHOSTS benchmark of natural-language graduate-level mathematics, with miniGHOSTS subset
Insight on which question types and domains (Chat)GPT is useful for, with failure modes (a 'mathematical model card')
Tracking of capability across versions: ChatGPT 9-Jan to 30-Jan, then GPT-4

method.summary: The authors wrote or sampled 709 prompts in six subdatasets, entered each by hand in the ChatGPT web UI (fresh session per prompt), and graded each output 1-5 with error and warning codes. ChatGPT 9-Jan and 30-Jan were run on all prompts, GPT-4 on a 170-prompt subset (miniGHOSTS).
method.task: Natural-language advanced mathematics: proofs, computation, fact retrieval, proof completion

datasets.name: Grad-Text
datasets.size: 130 prompts (Rudin FA ch1 28, ch2 15; Munkres ch1 37, ch2 29; Durrett 21)
datasets.source: Exercises from textbooks by Rudin, Munkres, Durrett; first/second chapters (Rudin only ch1 for [33] Durrett's book was limited to ch1); prompts not released (copyright), ref page given

datasets.name: Holes-in-Proofs
datasets.size: 162 prompts (Collection A 60; B Prealgebra 52; B Precalculus 50)
datasets.source: math.stackexchange, Axler and Rudin books, MATH; parts of proofs deleted
datasets.preprocessing: MISSING token, early finish, or explicit condition request

datasets.name: Olympiad-Problem-Solving
datasets.source: Engel, Problem-Solving Strategies; prompts drawn from all chapters; text-only problems

datasets.name: Symbolic-Integration
datasets.source: Test set of Lample & Charton 2019; CC BY-NC
datasets.preprocessing: converted by hand from Polish notation to LaTeX; checked with Mathematica and SymPy solutions

datasets.name: MATH
datasets.size: 138 prompts (Algebra 50, Counting and Probability 50, Prealgebra 18, Precalculus 20)
datasets.source: Hendrycks et al. MATH; MIT licence; equal number per difficulty level in Algebra and Probability

datasets.name: Search-Engine-Aspects
datasets.size: 78 prompts (Definition Retrieval 30, Reverse Definition Retrieval 30, Named Theorem Proof Completion 18)

datasets.name: miniGHOSTS
datasets.preprocessing: chosen so each 10-prompt subset has about the same mean and sd rating as its file (ChatGPT 30-Jan ratings), then manual pick for mathematical diversity

other.note: likely earlier instance of gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 (paper says 'likely')

models.name: ChatGPT 30-January-2023
models.architecture: as above; release notes claim improved factuality and mathematical capabilities

other.access: web GUI (API waitlist at the time)
other.version: not identified; paper lists API names gpt-4, gpt-4-0314, gpt-4-32k, gpt-4-32k-0314 as options

other.note: reported nearly 100% on 500 test equations [12, Table 3]; not rerun
best model about 50% on MATH [19, Table 3]; not rerun

inference.samples: one output per prompt per model version; no repeats reported
inference.prompting: Single prompt, no follow-up dialogue; new session per prompt; mostly LaTeX-encoded; prompt-engineered variant only for 24 Olympiad prompts (step-by-step, or 'Prove that...'/'Show that...')

other.temperature_and_settings: not controllable via web GUI and not known (App C)
other.stochasticity: authors note outputs are stochastic and may differ on the same prompt

metrics.name: Rating
metrics.definition: Expert score 1-5: 1 query not understood, 2 understood but entirely wrong, 3 partially correct, 4 mostly correct, 5 completely correct; 3.5 treated as pass threshold

metrics.name: Error codes
metrics.definition: e1 missing info, e2 few wrong/vague statements, e3 many wrong/vague, e4 wrong computation, e5 wrong logic (e5_1 to e5_5), e6 legal operations misunderstood; mandatory for ratings 2-4, none for 5

metrics.name: Warning codes
metrics.definition: w1 withholds essential info, w2 rambling, w3 hallucinating, w4 weird behaviour/opinionated, w5 changes notation

metrics.name: Confidence
metrics.definition: Perceived model confidence: high, medium, low

baselines: Lample & Charton model (numbers quoted from their paper)
eval.protocol: Graded by authors only (master's to professor level), harder prompts to more senior people; no third parties; fewer than 10 random samples per dataset re-rated by a second assessor; length outliers re-inspected; 95% confidence intervals in figures; sd uses Bessel's correction; no inter-annotator agreement reported.

availability.code: Python cleaning scripts available upon request
availability.data: github.com/xyfrieder/science-GHOSTS, CC BY-NC 4.0; copyrighted Grad-Text and Olympiad prompts withheld (ref key points to source)

results.claim: GPT-4 on miniGHOSTS has a substantially higher average rating than ChatGPT.
results.setup: miniGHOSTS (170 prompts), GPT-4 via web UI, expert ratings; sd 1.12
results.quote: which achieved a substantially higher average rating of 4.15 (standard deviation: 1.12)

results.claim: ChatGPT 9-Jan-2023 averages 3.20 on GHOSTS, below the 3.5 pass threshold.
results.setup: GHOSTS 709 prompts, ChatGPT 9-Jan-2023, no prompt-engineered items; sd 1.23
results.quote: the 9-January-2023 version achieves a rating of 3.20 with a standard deviation8 of 1.23

results.claim: ChatGPT 30-Jan-2023 averages 3.29, essentially the same as 9-Jan.
results.quote: overall performed similarly with an average rating of 3.29 (standard deviation: 1.28)

results.claim: On Symbolic-Integration, ChatGPT 9-Jan averages 2.51, far behind the specialised Lample-Charton model (nearly 100% on 500 test integrals).

results.quote: the 9-January-2023 version of ChatGPT achieves an average rating of 2.51 (standard deviation: 0.87)

results.quote: GPT-4 achieves an average of 3.50 (standard deviation: 1.43), barely a passing grade

results.claim: A rating of 2 dominates ChatGPT 9-Jan on integration prompts.
results.quote: a rating of 2 is dominating 70% of the time

results.claim: ChatGPT 9-Jan gets a perfect score on 29% of MATH samples; Minerva's best model gets 50% accuracy on MATH.
results.setup: MATH subdataset (138 prompts), ChatGPT 9-Jan; not comparable metrics (expert 5/5 vs final-answer accuracy)
results.note: Overall across all subdatasets 25% perfect for this version.
results.quote: achieves a perfect score only on 29% of our random samples from the MATH dataset

results.claim: GPT-4 gets rating 5 on 70% of MATH questions in miniGHOSTS.
results.quote: obtains a score of 5 on 70% of the corresponding questions within the miniGHOSTS dataset

results.claim: ChatGPT 9-Jan gets rating 5 on 25% of data points across all subdatasets.
results.quote: the total average of 25% of data points across all subdatasets in which this version achieves a perfect score

results.claim: On Reverse Definition Retrieval ChatGPT 9-Jan scores best, 4.30 average.
results.setup: Search-Engine-Aspects, Reverse Definition Retrieval file (30 prompts); sd 1.14
results.quote: with an average rating of 4.30 (standard deviation 1.14)

results.claim: On Olympiad-Problem-Solving 75% of ChatGPT 9-Jan scores are 2; no 5 and one 4.

results.claim: Wrong computations (e4) are the commonest error on MATH for ChatGPT 9-Jan.

results.claim: Prompt engineering (step-by-step or explicit 'Prove that') on Olympiad prompts lowered e2/e3/e4 errors but raised e5 logic errors and improved the mean rating only slightly.
results.setup: 24 prompt-engineered Olympiad prompts (about 20% of the subdataset), ChatGPT 9-Jan; effect read from Fig 3, no numbers in text

results.claim: Ratings shuffle between the two ChatGPT versions although grade counts stay similar; fewer than half of the prompts keep the same grade.
GHOSTS holds 709 prompts and miniGHOSTS 170; 1636 expert evaluations in total.
results.quote: in total (709+24)×2+170 = 1636 outputs and evaluations have been carried out

results.claim: GPT-4 passes (rating >=3.5) on miniGHOSTS files except Rudin ch.2 and Olympiad Problem Solving.
results.setup: miniGHOSTS, threshold 3.5; per-file bars read from Fig 1

results.claim: The authors state ChatGPT almost never voices uncertainty even when wrong, unlike Codex in one tested example.
results.setup: qualitative; one prompt on Unicode vs LaTeX equivalence (App D.3)

limits: ChatGPT and GPT-4 were accessed through the web GUI, so temperature and other settings are unknown and model versions are only identified by date (App C).
Grading is by the authors themselves, with a second look at fewer than 10 samples per dataset; no inter-rater agreement is reported.
GPT-4 was run only on miniGHOSTS (170 prompts, 10 per file), so its per-file averages rest on 10 prompts; authors call the GPT-4 findings preliminary.
Single run per prompt although outputs are stochastic.
Comparisons with Lample & Charton and Minerva use different metrics (1-5 expert rating vs final-answer accuracy) and different samples.
Dataset is too small to fine-tune on (authors); human grading cost prevents covering all field/question-type combinations.
Authors concede 'We are aware that these measures are not exhaustive' on human-error mitigation.
Possible training-data contamination is only argued, not tested (D1-D3 out-of-distribution tags).
Dated: GPT-4 and ChatGPT versions here are early 2023 models.
